title: Been slowly working on my first real game project, Threadbound, and finally recorded a short clip showing some of the current movement systems in-engine.
author: ThreadboundDev
selftext:
Been slowly working on my first real game project, *Threadbound*, and finally recorded a short clip showing some of the current movement systems in-engine.

Still very early and rough in a lot of areas, but this clip shows:

* basic movement
* grapple traversal
* wall cling
* jumping
* some early parallax/environment work
* and the general direction for the “flow-state” movement philosophy I’m aiming for

The core idea behind the game is a painterly 2D action-platformer / Metroidvania where movement and combat blend together continuously through real-time equipment swapping and momentum-based traversal.

A lot is still placeholder or being reworked (especially animation consistency), but it’s been really exciting finally seeing the systems start to come together visually instead of only existing in design docs and prototypes.

Would genuinely love feedback, especially from people who’ve worked on movement-heavy games before.

[Threadbound Early Movement](https://reddit.com/link/1tj6i2h/video/pm3jbbl4fe2h1/player)

replies.author: ThreadboundDev
replies.body: Thank you! It’s my first rodeo and I went straight for my “dream game” so it’s been a challenge! There is so much to do but it’s been fun!

comments.author: macuseri686
comments.body: Wow, this is seriously looking great so far! All the animations are flowing together fluidly! Also the parallax background looks cool!

replies.author: ThreadboundDev
replies.body: Thank you! I’m actually about to clean animations even more with rigging!

comments.author: PretendMirror8446
comments.body: Can you explain how you made the art? Are you an artist or everything is ai?

replies.author: ThreadboundDev
replies.body:
So some of both! I’ve found, and if you look close you’ll see, that ai struggles with consistency. It takes alot of prompts and uploading models + color palettes.

If I were to use gamelabs or sprite.io for everything then they would look consistent in color and shape, but they have issues as well like haloing!

So I generate some key frames and then edit them in krita as needed!

I’m actually about to transition to rigging to tackle this very issue!

replies.author: PretendMirror8446
replies.body: Thank you so much that's helpful..I didn't know about those tools I mainly try to do things myself without success since I'm a potato in anything art related 🤣

replies.author: ThreadboundDev
replies.body:
Honestly me too! My general workflow to this point has been to generate key frames with very precise prompts then I either take it into Krita OR go to gamelabsstudio. Gamelabs is a good tool, but you almost always have haloing and any animation outside of their predefined scope struggles a lot. 

For instance I wanted a more animie action style run as seen in the clip, but most generative ai run animations are very upright like a normal human. 

So I had to make a specific key frame to illustrate the style then make a sprite sheet in gamelabs. 

All these hoops and ladders have led me to the conclusion that if you want really cohesive art, the best option is probably rigging. That way the base is always the same and you can define the style.
